Spreading somewhat farther through tissue is not the same as being carried around the body in the blood.

Size is not what sets the speed; many neurotransmitters are small molecules.
Neurotransmitters work by binding receptors on the target cell, just as hormones do.
Traveling in the blood is endocrine signaling, the slower and broader route.

why.correct: Plasmodesmata connect the cytoplasms of plant cells through their walls, the plant counterpart of gap junctions, so small molecules pass straight from cell to cell.

why.correct: Kinase 2 total ÷ relay protein total = 500,000 ÷ 20 = 25,000. Equivalently 1,000 × 0.25 × 100 = 25,000.

The sensors are the skin's nerve endings that detect temperature.
The control center is the brain region that compares with the set point.
The stimulus is the rise in temperature itself.

why.correct: The loop compares temperature with the set point. At 37 °C the body is 2 °C below the new set point, so it responds as if cold: shivering and narrowed skin vessels raise temperature.
options: Below the new set point, the loop triggers heat-gaining responses.
Sweating is a response to being above the set point, which happens when the fever breaks.
The variable has not changed, but the set point has, so the gap triggers a response.
Raising the set point changes the target, not the sensitivity of the sensors; being below target triggers warming, not cooling.

why.correct: Positive feedback stops when an outside event removes the stimulus. Sealing the break covers the damaged wall that started the loop.
options: The loop ends when its trigger, the exposed damage, is gone.
Plenty of platelets remain; a clot uses a small fraction of them.
Opposing systems exist, but they do not reverse clotting the moment it starts; the clot must form first.
Positive feedback grows stronger with each cycle; it needs an outside event to stop.

why.correct: In both, the response opposes the change: glucose comes back down, temperature comes back down.
options: The response removes the stimulus (high glucose).
The response cancels the stimulus (high temperature).
Stronger contractions stretch the cervix more, adding to the change: positive feedback.
More ethylene causes more ripening and still more ethylene: positive feedback.
More platelets attract still more: positive feedback.

why.correct: Removing one arm of the glucose control system leaves nothing to oppose a fall in glucose; the other parts of the system are unchanged.

variables.name: Blood glucose
variables.why: Without glucagon, the falling glucose during the fast does not trigger the liver to release glucose, so it drops further than normal.

variables.name: Breakdown of glycogen in the liver
variables.why: Glucagon is the signal that makes liver cells break down glycogen; without it, less is broken down.

variables.name: Number of insulin receptors on muscle cells
variables.why: The condition affects glucagon release, not how many insulin receptors muscle cells make.

why.correct: The stimulus comes first; the beta cells respond with insulin; target cells remove glucose; the falling glucose removes the stimulus, so insulin falls: the loop switches itself off.
560 of 1,000 untreated cells have DNA content 1.0: they have not yet copied their DNA, so they are in G1 (or G0).
options: The tallest untreated bar is at 1.0, and unreplicated DNA means G1.
Only 200 untreated cells have content 2.0; that peak is the largest in the drug-treated culture.
Only 80 cells are at 1.5.
G1 cells have not copied their DNA, so their content is 1.0, not 2.0.

why.correct: Fraction in S = 240 ÷ 1,000 = 0.24. Time in S = 0.24 × 22 hours = 5.28, about 5.3 hours.
With drug Q, 720 of 1,000 cells have DNA content 2.0: they copied their DNA and then got stuck before dividing back to 1.0, as happens when the spindle cannot form.
options: A pile-up at 2.0 means copying finished but division did not.
Blocking copying would pile cells up at 1.0, not 2.0.
Copying twice would give cells at 4.0, and there are none.
Faster G1 would not leave cells stuck with doubled DNA; it would not change where cells finish.

why.correct: Cells already past S finish mitosis and return to 1.0; cells in G1 cannot copy their DNA. Over 18 hours the 2.0 peak drains and the 1.0 peak grows.
options: Without copying, cells collect at or near 1.0 and the 2.0 group empties.
That pattern belongs to drug Q, which blocks division, not copying.
Blocking copying acts in S phase, well before mitosis.
Cells cannot progress through S at all, so they do not spread out across it.

why.correct: Mitotic index = cells in mitosis ÷ total × 100 = 70 ÷ 200 × 100 = 35%.
Control: 20% in mitosis, 80% in interphase. Expected for 200 treated cells: 40 in mitosis, 160 in interphase. χ² = (70 − 40)² ÷ 40 + (130 − 160)² ÷ 160 = 22.5 + 5.625 = 28.1.
χ² = 28.1 is far above 3.84, so a difference this large would arise by chance less than 5% of the time if the chemical had no effect: reject the null hypothesis.
options: A chi-square value above the critical value means rejecting the null hypothesis.
This reverses the rule: a value above the critical value leads to rejecting the null.
A statistical test supports a difference; it does not prove a cause, and a higher index need not mean faster division.
The decision rests on the chi-square value compared with the critical value, not on one pair of counts.

why.correct: One tip from one bulb may be unusual. Replicate tips and bulbs show whether the difference holds across individuals.
options: Replication across tips and bulbs addresses the biggest weakness.
Recounting the same cells checks counting errors but not whether one bulb is typical.
Cells far from the tip divide little, which would hide any difference.
Unequal growing times would add a second difference between the groups.

why.correct: If cells divide more often, the treated roots make more cells and grow longer. If mitosis is just slower, the index rises but cell numbers and root growth do not.
options: Root growth reflects how many new cells are made, which separates the two ideas.
The number of chromosomes per cell is the same in both groups however often they divide.
Stain color tells nothing about how often cells divide.
The interphase percentage is just 100% minus the mitotic index, so it adds no new information.

why.correct: S phase copies each of the 6 chromosomes, so each has two sister chromatids: 6 × 2 = 12. The cell still has 6 chromosomes (6 centromeres).
DNA doubled in S phase, from 12 to 24 pg, and nothing has been separated into new cells by metaphase.
In anaphase the 12 sister chromatids separate; each now has its own centromere and counts as a chromosome: 12 in the cell, 6 moving to each pole.
Each pole received one copy of each of the 6 chromosomes, so each daughter cell is like the parent in G1: 6 chromosomes, 12 pg.
options: Mitosis gives daughter cells the same chromosomes and DNA as the parent had in G1.
Halving the parent's G1 number would leave each daughter cell missing chromosomes; mitosis halves only the doubled amount.
24 pg is the doubled amount before division, not what each daughter gets.
Twelve chromosomes is the count in the whole cell in anaphase, split between two cells.

why.correct: The actin ring makes the cleavage furrow. Mitosis still separates the chromosomes into two nuclei, but without cytokinesis they stay in one cell.
options: Nuclear division without cytoplasm division gives one cell with two nuclei.
Spindle attachment uses microtubules, which the drug does not affect.
Animal cells divide with a furrow; the cell plate is how plant cells divide.
The chromosomes are already enclosed in two new nuclei; a failed furrow does not remove them.

why.correct: A rigid wall surrounds each plant cell, so it cannot be pinched in two. Golgi vesicles fuse in the middle to make a plate that grows outward into new membrane and wall.
options: The wall is the reason; the plate builds a new wall between the two cells.
Plant cells do have actin; they divide by a plate because of the wall.
Plant cells do form a spindle, which separates chromatids before cytokinesis.
The chromosomes are inside new nuclei by then; a furrow divides cytoplasm, not chromosomes.

why.correct: Cells in G0 are not preparing to divide, so surviving nerve cells do not divide to replace lost ones.
options: Staying out of the cycle means no new nerve cells from division.
G0 cells left the cycle from G1 with a full, normal amount of DNA.
Cells in G0 are not dividing at all.
They left from G1, so they have the normal number of chromosomes.

why.correct: Budding in hydra (asexual reproduction) and wound healing (tissue repair) both make new cells by mitosis.
options: Budding is asexual reproduction by mitosis.
Wound healing is tissue repair by mitosis.
Bacteria divide by binary fission, without a nucleus or a spindle.
Viruses are copied by the host cell's machinery, not by cell division.
Losing a nucleus is not a division at all.

why.correct: A block in S phase stops new cells from reaching mitosis; cells past S are not affected, and the number of chromosomes per cell does not change.

variables.name: Number of cells completing mitosis
variables.why: Cells cannot finish S phase, so fewer and fewer reach mitosis once the cells already past S have divided.

variables.name: DNA content of a cell that was already in G2 when the drug was added
variables.why: That cell copied its DNA before the drug arrived, so it still has the doubled amount.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in a cell in G1
variables.why: Blocking copying does not add or remove chromosomes; a G1 cell has its normal set.

variables.name: Fraction of cells with doubled DNA content
variables.why: Cells with doubled DNA divide and are not replaced by new cells finishing S phase.

why.correct: Prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis: chromosomes must condense and attach before they can line up and separate.
CDK stays at 59-61 units throughout; cyclin climbs from 8 to 90 units over about 20 hours, then falls to 15 within an hour, twice.
options: Only cyclin cycles; CDK protein is flat.
CDK protein does not change.
This reverses the two proteins.
Both peak at mitosis, around 20 and 42 hours, not in S phase.

why.correct: Activity peaks at 20 and 42 hours, once per mitosis: 42 − 20 = 22 hours per cycle.
CDK never changes, so it cannot explain when activity rises; activity rises and falls with cyclin.
options: Activity tracks cyclin; CDK is constant.
CDK is flat, so it cannot set the timing.
Activity stays at 6 units or less until cyclin is above about 60 units, then jumps: it does not rise steadily with cyclin.
Activity of this mitotic cyclin-CDK peaks at mitosis, not in G1.

why.correct: Destroying cyclin is what switches CDK off so the cell can leave mitosis. With cyclin that stays, the complex stays active and the cells remain stuck in mitosis.
options: Entry needs high activity, which happens; exit needs cyclin destroyed, which cannot happen.
High mitotic cyclin-CDK drives mitosis, not a new round of copying.
The stem says this cyclin binds CDK normally.
The data show the timing follows cyclin, not CDK.

why.correct: Adding the activity and seeing whether mitosis follows tests cause, not just timing.
options: Changing the proposed cause and watching for the effect is a direct test.
Repeating the measurement would confirm the timing, not the cause.
The number of chromosomes is not changed by mitosis and says nothing about what triggers it.
Cells in G0 do not divide, so they cannot show what triggers mitosis.

why.correct: Line N: G1 rises from 45% to 74% and apoptosis from 1% to 18%. Line P stays at 38-44% in G1 and 1-3% apoptotic, like unexposed cells.
options: Only line N, with working p53, halts in G1 and dies by apoptosis.
Line P does not build up in G1, and its apoptosis stays near 1-3%.
This reverses the two lines.
Line N changes a great deal compared with its unexposed dishes (46% and 1%).

why.correct: Working p53 is the only difference between the lines. p53 halts the cycle at G1 (more cells in G1) and triggers apoptosis in cells it cannot save (rising apoptosis).
options: Both effects appear only where p53 works.
Line P received the same X-rays and did not stop, so X-rays do not halt cells directly.
p53 halts the cycle and switches on genes; it does not repair DNA itself.
Cells build up in G1 because they are held there, not because they move through S faster.

why.correct: Percent change = (74 − 45) ÷ 45 × 100 = 64.4%, about 64%.
Without p53, cells with damaged DNA neither stop for repair nor die; their damage is copied into daughter cells as mutations, which is how losing p53 raises cancer risk.
options: Skipping the halt and apoptosis lets damage become permanent mutations.
Line P shows almost no apoptosis, so damaged cells survive rather than die.
The dose was the same, but line N halted and removed damaged cells, so fewer mutations were passed on.
Line P cells keep cycling (38-44% in G1, like unexposed cells), so damaged DNA is copied.

why.correct: After 24 hours unexposed line N is still at 46% G1 and 1% apoptotic, so the rise in exposed dishes comes from the X-rays.
options: Same time, no X-rays, no change: the X-rays caused the effect.
The data give the fraction in G1, not growth rates; and that is not the comparison the control is for.
Cells do not move between dishes.
Unexposed cells have little damage to repair, and line N has p53.

why.correct: Sharing cytoplasm with an S cell starts DNA copying in a G1 nucleus, and sharing with an M cell makes another nucleus condense its chromosomes: something in the cytoplasm drives each phase.
options: The second nucleus changes according to the other cell's phase, through the shared cytoplasm.
The G1 nuclei change their timing immediately after fusion, so the shared cytoplasm matters.
The G1 nuclei follow the other cell's lead, not the reverse.
S + G1 fusions lead to DNA copying, not to mitosis.

why.correct: The same S-phase cytoplasm starts copying in a G1 nucleus but not in a G2 nucleus, so the difference lies in the nucleus itself: once copied, DNA is not copied again until after mitosis.
options: The difference between the G1 and G2 nuclei shows a block in the already-copied nucleus.
The G1 nucleus responded to the S signal without its own S-phase cyclin, so the G2 nucleus's cyclin level is not what decided this.
Nuclei in every phase of interphase have pores; G2 nuclei exchange molecules with the cytoplasm.
Nothing suggests damage, and the G2 nucleus entered mitosis on schedule.

why.correct: MPF acts by phosphorylating target proteins. With its kinase activity blocked, the M-phase signal is gone, so the G2 nucleus is not pushed into mitosis.
options: No kinase activity, no phosphorylated targets, no condensation.
Cyclin works only by switching on the CDK's kinase activity, which is blocked.
Blocking CDK does not reset a nucleus that has already copied its DNA.
Cyclin acts through its CDK; on its own it does not condense chromosomes.

why.correct: G1 cyclin-CDK carries the cell past the G1 checkpoint into S phase. Blocked, the cancer cells stay in G1.
options: The G1 cyclin-CDK acts at the G1 checkpoint, so the block holds cells there.
That would follow from keeping mitotic cyclin-CDK active, a different complex.
Blocking the G1 complex stops entry into S, so no copying happens at all.
Without the G1 push, cells do not leave G1, so they divide less.

why.correct: One overactive copy pushes division by itself. A brake fails only when no working copy is left to make the brake protein.
options: Gain of an accelerator takes one copy; loss of a brake takes two.
Body cells carry two copies of nearly every gene, proto-oncogenes included.
Every gene is copied once in S phase.
Both kinds of mutation are copied into daughter cells by mitosis.

why.correct: Contact inhibition stops division where cells touch on all sides. Cells at the new edge lose that contact, divide into the gap and stop once it is filled.
options: Division happens where contact is lost and stops when it returns.
Cells away from the strip still touch neighbors, and normal cells do not pile up.
Normal cells resume dividing when contact is lost, as in wound healing.
Losing neighbors does not damage DNA; it removes a stop signal.

why.correct: Malignant tumors invade nearby tissue and spread (metastasis); cells growing in the liver show that spread has begun.
options: Invasion and spread define a malignant tumor.
Benign tumors also grow by extra division; fast division alone does not show spread.
A contained, stable tumor fits the description of a benign one.
Every dividing body cell has a nucleus and copies its DNA.

why.correct: A stuck-on receptor is an oncogene (accelerator on); losing p53 removes a brake and the apoptosis that removes damaged cells.
options: A receptor stuck on drives division without the signal.
Without p53, damaged cells neither halt nor die.
Less G1 cyclin means less CDK activity, so fewer cells pass the G1 checkpoint.
More brake protein slows division.
Caspases carry out apoptosis, which removes cells.

why.correct: The M checkpoint guards chromosome sharing. Without it, mitosis is faster but mistakes in sharing get through; earlier events are unaffected.

variables.name: Chance that a daughter cell gets the wrong number of chromosomes
variables.why: A chromosome whose sisters are not attached to both poles can be pulled to one pole, so one daughter gets an extra copy and the other is missing one.

variables.name: Time a cell spends in metaphase when one chromosome is slow to attach
variables.why: Normally the cell waits for the late chromosome; without the checkpoint it does not wait.

variables.name: Amount of DNA copied in S phase
variables.why: The M checkpoint acts in mitosis; copying in S phase is unchanged.

variables.name: Number of centrosomes formed before mitosis
variables.why: Centrosomes are copied before mitosis, independently of the checkpoint that checks attachment.

why.correct: Damage raises p53; p53 first halts the cycle by blocking cyclin-CDK; only if repair fails does it trigger apoptosis, which caspases carry out.
